title: Morning Edition
dek: Yemen’s renewed west-coast war has displaced more than 100,000 people and pushed thousands across the sea to Djibouti; deaths in Nigerian paramilitary custody trigger protests and an investigation; Japan raises rates to a 31-year high; and the Ideas desk moves from ancient households to African philosophy.

lead_story.headline: Yemen’s renewed west-coast fighting has displaced more than 100,000 people and pushed thousands across the sea to Djibouti
lead_story.summary: IOM says displacement from the escalation that began in June has climbed above 100,000, concentrated in Taiz and Lahj, while thousands of Yemenis have crossed the Gulf of Aden toward Djibouti. The latest Reuters count is about 112,000 internally displaced and nearly 3,000 who have fled by sea.
lead_story.why_it_matters: The territorial fight around Yemen’s Red Sea coast is now producing a fast-moving civilian displacement crisis on top of a country already weakened by years of war. The exact total is changing quickly as IOM updates field tracking, so the direction and scale are firmer than any single daily count.

items.headline: At least 33 suspected illegal miners died in Nigerian paramilitary custody, and the cause remains disputed
items.summary: Detainees arrested during illegal-mining raids in Niger State were found dead in custody of the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps. The agency first referred to a suspected disease outbreak, later said the cause had not been established, and the interior minister suspended the state commandant while an investigation proceeds.
items.why_it_matters: The central fact is mass death in state custody, not the mining allegation. Nigerian reporting and international coverage disagree on the exact toll—33, 37 or 40—while survivors cited by AP described suffocation. A medical cause has not yet been established, so the edition uses the lowest directly documented count and keeps competing explanations attributed.

items.headline: Japan raised its policy rate to 1.25%, the highest level in 31 years
items.summary: The Bank of Japan voted 7–2 to lift its short-term policy rate from 1% to about 1.25%, continuing its exit from decades of near-zero borrowing costs. Two board members dissented.
items.why_it_matters: Japan was the extreme case of ultra-low interest rates. A 1.25% policy rate is still modest by many countries’ standards, but the normalization changes borrowing costs, the yen and the economics of Japan’s very large public debt. The decision was widely expected; the more important signal is how far the bank is willing to continue.

items.headline: Fewer people are reaching Europe by sea this year, but more are dying or disappearing on the routes
items.summary: IOM says sea arrivals were down 39% year-on-year by mid-September, to about 60,000, while at least 2,292 people had died or gone missing, up from 1,999 over the comparable period last year. The agency cautions that the real death toll is probably higher.
items.why_it_matters: A falling arrival count can look like a successful border statistic while masking a worsening risk per journey. The pattern is especially important because route changes, rescue capacity, smuggling practices and enforcement can alter danger independently of how many people attempt the crossing.

items.headline: Cuba’s electrical grid collapsed nationwide for the sixth time this year in early August
items.summary: On August 2–3, Cuba’s national grid suffered another total disconnection and then failed again during restoration. The episode followed three nationwide failures in July and came amid severe fuel shortages, aging thermal plants and chronic maintenance problems.
items.why_it_matters: A blackout is temporary; repeated whole-system collapse is an infrastructure condition. The crisis affects water pumping, refrigeration, hospitals, communications and ordinary sleep during summer heat. Cuba attributes much of the strain to U.S. sanctions and fuel restrictions; independent reporting also points to old equipment, underinvestment and maintenance failures.
items.original_language: English; Spanish-language Cuban and regional reporting checked

items.headline: Political philosophy may have made the household too private to think about clearly
items.summary: Sandrine Bergès argues that ancient political philosophy treated the household as a genuine community with questions of authority, dependence, work and shared goods—not merely as a private refuge outside politics. Recovering that tradition changes what counts as a political problem.
items.why_it_matters: The household is where people first encounter care, dependency, unequal power and the division of labor. Treating it as conceptually separate from public life can hide political assumptions inside supposedly private arrangements. The harder question is how to recognize the household’s political structure without making every intimate relationship an arm of the state.
items.country: United Kingdom / ancient Mediterranean intellectual history

items.headline: An urban Mbya Guaraní school in Paraguay turned its annual fair into a three-language classroom for local culture
items.summary: At Yva Viju Miri school in Ciudad del Este, students prepared work on food, games, medicinal plants, stories, history and poetry in Mbya Guaraní, Spanish and Guaraní for the school’s annual pedagogical fair.
items.why_it_matters: The stakes are deliberately local: a school making room for children to research and present the knowledge around them in the languages they actually inherit. Recent Human Scale stops moved through Indonesia, Zimbabwe, Gabon, the Philippines and France; this shifts the lane to a Paraguayan Indigenous urban community and Latin America.
items.country: Paraguay — Ciudad del Este, Alto Paraná
items.original_language: Spanish / Mbya Guaraní and Guaraní content described

worth_your_time.headline: How one philosopher tried to rebuild African philosophy without making Europe either its master or its enemy
worth_your_time.summary: An Aeon essay on Lansana Keita traces a philosophical project that is Afrocentric without treating African thought as intellectually sealed off from other traditions. Keita combines criticism of inherited colonial categories with engagement across economics, science and the Western canon.
worth_your_time.why_it_matters: The piece is useful because it avoids two easy stories: that philosophy is a universal European inheritance simply exported elsewhere, or that intellectual decolonization requires refusing outside traditions. Keita’s harder proposal is reconstruction—asking what philosophical institutions and arguments should serve African societies now while remaining open to criticism from anywhere.

editorial_review.repetition_check: pass with one threshold-crossing Yemen return — Yemen returns because the earlier territorial shift at Bab el-Mandeb has now produced a rapidly growing displacement emergency; yesterday’s Iran accountability, South Sudan election administration, Korea–Central Asia minerals and Congo Ebola are not repeated.

Non-U.S. sources were searched first across Latin America, Africa and Asia. editorial_review.discovery_check: pass — custodial accountability in Niger State, migration-route mortality, Cuban grid fragility, domestic political philosophy and African intellectual history widen the edition beyond the dominant Iran conflict.
editorial_review.long_read_check: pass — the long read is durable intellectual history/philosophy and independent of current affairs.
editorial_review.triangulation_check: pass with explicit uncertainty — Yemen combines Reuters with IOM’s primary displacement tracking and independent regional reporting; Nigeria combines Reuters, AP, Nigerian local reporting and the NSCDC/government account while preserving disagreement over toll and cause; Japan combines Reuters/AP with the Bank of Japan’s own decision; European migration uses Reuters/AP plus IOM data; Cuba combines Reuters/AP/AFP-derived reporting with Cuban state-utility statements. No participant explanation is presented as established when the evidence remains contested.
editorial_review.difference_from_recent: The paper moves from wartime legal accountability and election administration toward the civilian consequences of Yemen’s renewed fighting, deaths in state custody, monetary normalization, migration-route risk, infrastructure fragility and two durable questions about community and intellectual inheritance.
notes_for_next_edition: Yemen should return for a major new displacement threshold, cross-border refugee emergency, navigation change, ceasefire/counteroffensive or another verified territorial shift—not routine daily counts.
Nigeria custodial deaths should return for autopsy findings, an independent inquiry, charges or a credible official account of cause—not protest reaction alone.
Bank of Japan should return for a materially new policy signal, yen intervention or clear economic consequence—not routine market moves.
European migration mortality should return for materially updated route data or a policy/rescue change that helps explain the risk shift.

Human Scale should continue non-U.S.-first rotation and avoid returning immediately to Europe, Southeast Asia or southern Africa if a strong Middle Eastern, Caribbean, island or East Asian local story clears the bar.
